title: Wishes, requests and purpose with 'щоб'
objectives: I can say what I want someone else to do with 'щоб' and the past form, and what I want to do myself with an infinitive.
I can say why someone does something with 'щоб', 'для того́, щоб' and 'за́мість того́, щоб'.
I can ask, demand, insist, allow, forbid and suggest with 'проси́ти', 'вимага́ти', 'наполяга́ти', 'дозволя́ти', 'забороня́ти' and 'пропонува́ти', and pass on a request with 'Скажи́ йому́, щоб...'.
I can say what is important or necessary with 'важли́во' and 'необхі́дно', and express hopes and fears with 'сподіва́тися, що' and 'боя́тися, що'.
I can explain why 'щоб' is one word, why 'бої́шся' is written with 'ї', and why the imperative of 'боя́тися' is 'бі́йся'.

vocabulary.source: so that, in order to; that, after wishes
vocabulary.note: 'Що' and the particle 'б' of the conditional, written as one word. When its clause has a subject of its own, the verb is the past form; in a clause of purpose without its own subject, the verb is an infinitive. Inside a sentence a comma stands before it.

example.target: Я говорю́ пові́льно, щоб ти все розумі́в.
example.source: I'm speaking slowly so that you understand everything.
example.source_literal: I speak slowly, that-would you everything understood.

vocabulary.note: 'Прошу́', 'про́сиш', 'про́сять': 'с' becomes 'ш' only in the 'я' form. Perfective partner 'попроси́ти' ('попрошу́', 'попро́сиш'). The person asked is in the accusative, and what is asked for is an infinitive or a clause with 'щоб'. The form 'прошу́' alone is also said politely when you invite someone in or hand something over: 'Прошу́, захо́дьте.' (Please come in.)

example.source: I'm asking you to help Mom.

vocabulary.note: 'Вимага́ю', 'вимага́єш', like 'чита́ти'. The person from whom something is demanded follows 'від' with the genitive ('від ме́не', 'від нас'). What is demanded is a noun in the genitive ('Ця робо́та вимага́є ча́су.', This work takes time) or a clause with 'щоб'. It has no perfective partner in everyday use.

example.target: Іри́на Петрі́вна вимага́є, щоб ми говори́ли украї́нською.
example.source: Iryna Petrivna demands that we speak Ukrainian.
example.source_literal: Iryna Petrivna demands, that-would we spoke by-Ukrainian.

vocabulary.note: Perfective partner 'побажа́ти'. The person is in the dative and the thing wished in the genitive: 'Бажа́ю тобі́ ща́стя!' (I wish you happiness!) A wish about an action takes a clause with 'щоб'.

Perfective partner 'дозво́лити' ('дозво́лю', 'дозво́лиш'; imperative 'дозво́ль', 'дозво́льте'). The person allowed is in the dative and the action is an infinitive. 'Дозво́льте...' opens a polite offer: 'Дозво́льте вам допомогти́.' (Let me help you.)

example.source: The doctor allows Sam to go for walks.

vocabulary.note: 'Забороня́ю', 'забороня́єш', like 'чита́ти'. Perfective partner 'заборони́ти'. As with 'дозволя́ти', the person is in the dative and the action is an infinitive. The noun 'заборо́на' means a ban.

example.target: Батьки́ не забороня́ють ді́тям гра́ти у футбо́л.
example.source: The parents don't forbid the children to play soccer.
example.source_literal: Parents not forbid to-children to-play in soccer.

vocabulary.note: Perfective partner 'наполягти́'. What someone insists on follows 'на' with the locative. Before a clause it is 'на то́му, щоб', where 'то́му' is the locative of 'те' and points ahead to the clause; the conjunction 'тому́', therefore, has the same letters and another stress.

example.target: Та́то наполяга́є на то́му, щоб ми пої́хали по́їздом.
example.source: Dad insists that we go by train.
example.source_literal: Dad insists on that, that-would we went by-train.

vocabulary.note: 'Пропону́ю', 'пропону́єш': '-ува-' becomes '-у-', as in 'працюва́ти'. Perfective partner 'запропонува́ти'. It takes the person in the dative and the thing offered in the accusative. The action suggested is an infinitive, often for something the speaker will share ('Пропону́ю піти́ в кіно́.', I suggest we go to the movies), or a clause with 'щоб' that has its own subject.

example.source: Andrii is offering us a new salad.

vocabulary.note: Like 'тре́ба', it is the predicate of a sentence without a grammatical subject. The person to whom something matters is in the dative. The adjective 'важли́вий' has its stress on another syllable.

example.target: Мені́ ду́же важли́во, щоб ти прийшла́.
example.source: It's very important to me that you come.
example.source_literal: To-me very important, that-would you came.

vocabulary.note: It means the same as 'тре́ба' but is more formal, and it is common in rules, instructions and official speech. The adjective is 'необхі́дний', with the same stress.

example.source: It is necessary that everyone knows this.

vocabulary.note: Built from the preposition 'для', the genitive 'того́' of 'те', and 'щоб'. It means the same as 'щоб' in a clause of purpose but gives the purpose more weight, and it is common in writing.

example.target: Сем живе́ в Ки́єві для того́, щоб вивча́ти украї́нську мо́ву.
example.source: Sam lives in Kyiv in order to learn Ukrainian.
example.source_literal: Sam lives in Kyiv for that, that-would to-study Ukrainian language.

vocabulary.note: It takes the genitive. Before an action it becomes 'за́мість того́, щоб' with an infinitive: 'За́мість того́ щоб відпочива́ти, він працю́є.' (Instead of resting, he is working.)

example.source: Today Sofiia is working instead of Taras.

vocabulary.note: It names a result you work toward. Instrumental 'мето́ю': 'З яко́ю мето́ю?' (For what purpose?), literally 'with which aim?'.

example.source: What is the purpose of your trip?

vocabulary.note: What you hope will be true follows in a clause with 'що': 'Є наді́я, що...' (There is hope that...). It is also a woman's name, 'Наді́я'.

example.target: У нас є наді́я, що Окса́на нам допомо́же.
example.source: We have hope that Oksana will help us.
example.source_literal: At us is hope, that Oksana to-us will-help.

vocabulary.note: 'Сподіва́юся', 'сподіва́єшся'. Its '-ся' adds no meaning of doing something to oneself, so 'сподіва́юся' is glossed 'I-hope'. It takes 'що' with the indicative, or 'на' with the accusative for what you count on: 'Я сподіва́юся на вас.' (I'm counting on you.) 'Сподіва́юся.' alone means 'I hope so'. It has no perfective partner.

'Бою́ся', 'бої́шся', 'бої́ться', 'боїмо́ся', 'боїте́ся', 'боя́ться'; imperative 'не бі́йся', 'не бі́йтеся'. What you fear is in the genitive, what you are afraid to do is an infinitive, and what you fear will be true is a clause with 'що'. It has no perfective partner.

example.source: The children aren't afraid of the doctor.

dialogues.title: Dinner on Sunday
dialogues.context: Oksana's mother Halyna phones her about a family dinner on Sunday. They say 'ти' to each other, and Oksana calls her 'ма́мо'.

lines.source_literal: Oksana, on Sunday at us dinner. I want, that-would you came.

lines.source_literal: Therefore I ask you: tell to-him today, that-would he nothing not planned for Sunday.

lines.speaker: Окса́на

lines.source_literal: At seventh. Important, that-would you came together, because dad not likes to-wait.

lines.speaker: Окса́на

lines.source_literal: Mom, and why this so important?

lines.speaker: Гали́на

lines.source: Because you talk about him very often. I want him to feel at home with us.
lines.source_literal: Because you very often about him talk. I want, that-would he felt at us as at-home.

lines.speaker: Окса́на

lines.speaker: Окса́на

lines.source_literal: I-hope, that Sam will-be free. I to-him today will-phone.

dialogues.title: Finished by Friday
dialogues.context: Sofiia, Taras's colleague, now manages his team at work. The company's director ('дире́ктор') is waiting for their new project ('проє́кт'), and on Monday morning Sofiia comes to Taras's desk. They have always said 'ти' to each other.

lines.speaker: Со́фія
lines.target: Тара́се, до́брий ра́нок. Мені́ тре́ба, щоб ми закі́нчили проє́кт до п’я́тниці.

lines.source_literal: Taras, good morning. To-me needed, that-would we finished project until Friday.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: До п’я́тниці? Со́фіє, це ду́же ма́ло ча́су!

lines.speaker: Со́фія

lines.speaker: Тара́с

lines.speaker: Со́фія
lines.target: До́бре, так і зро́бимо. І ще: я забороня́ю вам працюва́ти вночі́. Важли́во, щоб ви спа́ли!

lines.target: Дя́кую, Со́фіє. Сподіва́юся, що в п’я́тницю ми вже бу́демо відпочива́ти.

grammar.title: Wishes about someone else: 'щоб' with the past form
grammar.explanation:
When you want to do something yourself, the verb of wanting is followed by an infinitive, as in English: 'Я хо́чу прийти́.' (I want to come.) The person who wants and the person who comes are the same, and neither language names that person twice.

When you want another person to do something, English says 'I want you to come', with the other person as the object of 'want' and an infinitive after it. Ukrainian does not build the sentence this way. It makes a second clause, a part of the sentence with its own subject and its own verb, and joins it to the first with the conjunction 'щоб': 'Я хо́чу, щоб ти прийшо́в.' (I want you to come), literally 'I want, that-would you came'. A conjunction is a word that joins clauses, like 'і', 'але́' and 'якщо́'.

'Щоб' is 'що', that, fused with the particle 'б' of the conditional, just as 'якби́' is 'як' fused with 'би'. Because it contains the particle, the clause after it is a conditional: it presents the action as wanted, not as a fact. Its verb is therefore the past form, exactly as after 'би', and it takes no second 'б'. The past form agrees in gender and number with the subject of its own clause, not with the person who wants:

- 'Я хо́чу, щоб ти прийшо́в.' (I want you to come), said to a man
- 'Я хо́чу, щоб ти прийшла́.' (I want you to come), said to a woman
- 'Ма́ма хо́че, щоб ми прийшли́ ра́зом.' (Mom wants us to come together.)
- 'Я хо́чу, щоб було́ те́пло.' (I want it to be warm), with the 'воно́' form in a clause without a subject

As in every conditional, the past form carries no past time. 'Я хо́чу, щоб ти прийшо́в за́втра.' (I want you to come tomorrow) is about tomorrow. The time of the wish comes from the verb of wanting: 'Я хоті́в, щоб ти прийшо́в.' means 'I wanted you to come'. Because the past form shows gender and number but not person, a clause with 'щоб' always names its subject, by a pronoun or a noun: 'щоб ти прийшо́в', 'щоб він прийшо́в', 'щоб Сем прийшо́в'. Only a clause without a subject, such as 'щоб було́ те́пло', names none.

The choice therefore depends only on the subjects. One subject for both actions takes the infinitive; two different subjects take 'щоб' and the past form. Compare 'Я хо́чу відпочива́ти.' (I want to rest) with 'Я хо́чу, щоб ти відпочива́в.' (I want you to rest). Aspect is chosen as everywhere else: the perfective for one completed act ('щоб ти прийшо́в'), the imperfective for a process or a habit ('Я хо́чу, щоб ти ча́сто дзвони́в.', I want you to phone often). A comma always separates the clause with 'щоб' from the main clause.

The polite 'Я б хоті́в...' and 'Я б хоті́ла...' take 'щоб' in the same way: 'Я б хоті́ла, щоб ви прийшли́.' (I would like you to come.) A clause with 'щоб' can also stand alone as a wish, with 'I want' or 'I wish' left unsaid: 'Щоб ти був здоро́вий!' (May you be healthy!), literally 'that-would you were healthy!'. The culture note shows how often this is heard at the table.

rows: I want it to be warm.
Я б хоті́ла, щоб ви прийшли́.
I would wanted, that-would you came
I would like you to come.

examples.source_literal: Taras wants, that-would Olena to-him phoned.

examples.source_literal: I not want, that-would you waited.

examples.target: Що ти хо́чеш, щоб я зроби́в?
examples.source: What do you want me to do?
examples.source_literal: What you want, that-would I did?

examples.target: Я хоті́в, щоб ти прочита́ла цю кни́гу.
examples.source: I wanted you to read this book.
examples.source_literal: I wanted, that-would you read this book.

examples.target: Щоб ти був здоро́вий!

examples.source_literal: That-would you were healthy!

grammar.title: Purpose: 'щоб', 'для того́, щоб' and 'за́мість того́, щоб'
grammar.explanation:
A clause of purpose says what an action is meant to achieve. English says 'I study Ukrainian to work in Ukraine' or 'in order to work'. Ukrainian uses the same conjunction 'щоб' as for wishes, and the same rule about subjects decides what follows it.

When the purpose has the same subject as the main clause, 'щоб' takes an infinitive: 'Я вивча́ю украї́нську мо́ву, щоб працюва́ти в Украї́ні.' (I study Ukrainian to work in Ukraine), literally 'I study Ukrainian language, that-would to-work in Ukraine'. English can say purpose with 'to' alone, but Ukrainian normally needs 'щоб' before the infinitive. After a verb of motion the bare infinitive is also common: 'Я прийшо́в тобі́ допомогти́.' and 'Я прийшо́в, щоб тобі́ допомогти́.' both mean 'I came to help you'.

When another person or thing is to act, 'щоб' takes the past form with its own subject, as after 'хоті́ти': 'Я говорю́ пові́льно, щоб ти все розумі́в.' (I speak slowly so that you understand everything.) Again the past form says nothing about time.

A negative purpose is 'щоб не', 'so as not to' or 'so that ... not':

- 'Я п’ю ка́ву, щоб не спа́ти.' (I drink coffee so as not to fall asleep.)
- 'Візьми́ ку́ртку, щоб тобі́ не було́ хо́лодно.' (Take a jacket so that you don't get cold), literally 'that-would to-you not was cold', with the predicative word 'хо́лодно' in a clause without a subject

'Для того́, щоб' (in order to) is a longer form of 'щоб' that gives the purpose more weight. It is built from the preposition 'для', for, and 'того́', the genitive of the demonstrative pronoun 'те', which points ahead to the clause: literally 'for that, that-would'. It is common in careful speech and in writing, and it can open the sentence: 'Для того́ щоб до́бре говори́ти, тре́ба бага́то говори́ти.' (To speak well, you need to speak a lot.) Inside a sentence the comma usually stands before 'щоб'; a conjunction that opens the sentence is not split, and the comma follows its whole clause.

'За́мість того́, щоб' (instead of) with an infinitive names an action that does not happen in place of one that does: 'За́мість того́ щоб відпочива́ти, він працю́є.' (Instead of resting, he is working), literally 'instead of-that that-would to-rest'. 'За́мість' itself is a preposition that takes the genitive, and with a noun it needs no clause: 'Я п’ю сік за́мість ка́ви.' (I drink juice instead of coffee.) English uses the '-ing' form after 'instead of'; Ukrainian uses the infinitive after 'за́мість того́, щоб'.

To ask about purpose, say 'З яко́ю мето́ю?' (For what purpose?), literally 'with which aim?', with the instrumental of 'мета́'. In everyday speech the simple 'Чому́?' (Why?) is more common, and the answer may begin with 'щоб'.

grammar.title: Requests, demands, permission and necessity
grammar.explanation:
Verbs that ask, tell or allow someone to act work like 'хоті́ти': the action asked for can go into a clause with 'щоб' and the past form, with its own subject. Several of them can also take the person in a case and an infinitive. Each verb keeps its own case for the person, and the case is learned with the verb:

- 'проси́ти' (to ask, to request) takes the person in the accusative and an infinitive, or a clause with 'щоб': 'Я прошу́ тебе́ прийти́.' and 'Я прошу́, щоб ти прийшо́в.' both mean 'I'm asking you to come'
- 'вимага́ти' (to demand) takes the person after 'від' with the genitive, and what is demanded in a clause with 'щоб': 'Вона́ вимага́є від нас, щоб ми прийшли́.' (She demands that we come.)
- 'наполяга́ти' (to insist) takes 'на' with the locative; before a clause it is 'на то́му, щоб', with the locative 'то́му' of 'те' pointing ahead, literally 'on that, that-would': 'Він наполяга́є на то́му, щоб ми прийшли́.' (He insists that we come.)
- 'дозволя́ти' (to allow) and 'забороня́ти' (to forbid) take the person in the dative and an infinitive: 'Лі́кар забороня́є Се́мові пи́ти ка́ву.' (The doctor forbids Sam to drink coffee.)
- 'пропонува́ти' (to suggest, to offer) takes an infinitive, often for something the speaker will share ('Пропону́ю піти́ в кіно́.', I suggest we go to the movies), or a clause with 'щоб' that has its own subject ('Пропону́ю, щоб ти пої́хав зі мно́ю.', I suggest you come with me)
- 'сказа́ти' and 'каза́ти' with 'щоб' pass on a request or an order: 'Скажи́ йому́, щоб він зайшо́в.' (Tell him to drop in.)

The last verb shows the difference between 'що' and 'щоб' most clearly. 'Що' introduces a fact, with the verb in the tense the meaning needs. 'Щоб' introduces an action that someone wants done, with the past form:

- 'Він сказа́в, що Окса́на прийшла́.' (He said that Oksana had come), a fact
- 'Він сказа́в, щоб Окса́на прийшла́.' (He said Oksana should come), a request

Predicative words of importance and necessity also take 'щоб'. A predicative word is the whole predicate of a sentence without a grammatical subject, as 'тре́ба' and 'шко́да' are. With an infinitive it says what is needed, with the person who must act in the dative: 'Мені́ тре́ба працюва́ти.' (I need to work.) With 'щоб' and the past form the person who must act becomes the subject of a clause of its own:

- 'Важли́во, щоб ти до́бре спав.' (It's important that you sleep well.)
- 'Необхі́дно, щоб усі́ це зна́ли.' (It's necessary that everyone knows this.)
- 'Мені́ тре́ба, щоб ти мені́ допомі́г.' (I need you to help me), literally 'to-me needed, that-would you to-me helped'

'Важли́во' and 'необхі́дно' are not adverbs here: nothing in the sentence is a verb they could describe. 'Необхі́дно' is more formal than 'тре́ба' and is typical of rules and instructions.

grammar.title: Hope and fear: 'що' with the indicative
grammar.explanation:
'Щоб' is for actions that someone wants, asks for or aims at. Hope and fear are different: the speaker expects that something is or will be true, or fears it, and Ukrainian states that thing as a fact. The clause opens with 'що', that, and its verb is in the indicative, the mood of ordinary statements, in whatever tense the meaning needs:

- 'Я сподіва́юся, що ти при́йдеш.' (I hope you'll come), with the perfective future 'при́йдеш'
- 'Я бою́ся, що він не при́йде.' (I'm afraid he won't come.)
- 'Сподіва́юся, що вам сподо́балося.' (I hope you liked it), with the past

English often uses the present after 'I hope' even for the future ('I hope you come'), but Ukrainian uses the future for a future event, as it does after 'якщо́' and 'коли́'.

'Сподіва́тися' is a reflexive verb whose '-ся' adds no meaning of doing something to oneself, so 'сподіва́юся' is glossed 'I-hope'. Alone, 'Сподіва́юся.' means 'I hope so'. With 'на' and the accusative it means 'to hope for' or 'to count on': 'Я сподіва́юся на вас.' (I'm counting on you.) The noun 'наді́я', hope, takes 'що' in the same way: 'Є наді́я, що за́втра не бу́де дощу́.' (There is hope that it won't rain tomorrow.)

'Боя́тися' (to be afraid) has three constructions, chosen by what is feared:

- a thing or a person, in the genitive: 'Кіт бої́ться води́.' (The cat is afraid of water.)
- an action the subject is afraid to do, as an infinitive: 'Я бою́ся ї́здити вночі́.' (I'm afraid to travel at night.)
- something the subject fears is or will be true, in a clause with 'що': 'Я бою́ся, що ми не закі́нчимо.' (I'm afraid we won't finish.)

Its imperative is 'не бі́йся' to one person you call 'ти' and 'не бі́йтеся' to others; the spelling note explains the form.

Set side by side, the two conjunctions show the two moods:

- 'Я хо́чу, щоб він прийшо́в.' (I want him to come.) The speaker wants the action: 'щоб' and the past form, the conditional.
- 'Я сподіва́юся, що він при́йде.' (I hope he'll come.) The speaker expects a fact: 'що' and the future, the indicative.

The verb also shows which conjunction is meant: after 'щоб' it is always the past form or an infinitive, never a present or a future form.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: 'щоб', 'бої́шся', 'бі́йся', 'прошу́' and 'важли́во'
grammar.explanation:
'Щоб' is written as one word because it is one conjunction: 'що' and the particle 'б' have fused, as 'як' and 'би' have in 'якби́'. It is said as one syllable, [ʃt͡ʃɔb], and its final 'б' stays voiced, as in 'хліб'. Written as two words, 'що б' is the question word 'що', what, followed by the particle of a conditional verb: 'Що б ти зроби́в?' (What would you do?) The test taught in the unit on the conditional tells them apart: in 'що б' the particle can move to the verb ('Що ти зроби́в би?'), while 'щоб' cannot be split.

'Боя́тися' belongs to the second conjugation, like 'стоя́ти', and its stem 'бо-' ends in a vowel. After a vowel, the endings '-у', '-иш', '-ить' and '-ать' of this conjugation are written with 'ю', 'ї' and 'я', each of which stands for [j] and a vowel, as the alphabet units taught:

- 'бою́ся' [bɔˈjusʲɑ], with 'ю' [ju] after 'о'
- 'бої́шся' [bɔˈjisʲːɑ], with 'ї', which is always [ji], and '-шся' said [sʲːɑ], as in 'прокида́єшся'
- 'бої́ться' [bɔˈjit͡sʲːɑ], with '-ться' said [t͡sʲːɑ]
- 'боя́ться' [bɔˈjɑt͡sʲːɑ], the 'вони́' form

The imperative 'бі́йся' follows the rule for a stem that ends in a vowel: the stem 'бо-' takes '-й', as 'чита́-' gives 'чита́й'. The '-й' closes the syllable, and in a closed syllable 'о' becomes 'і', as in 'кіт' against 'кота́'. So the stem becomes 'бій', and with '-ся' the imperative is 'бі́йся', plural 'бі́йтеся'. 'Стоя́ти' does the same: 'стій'.

'Проси́ти' changes 'с' to 'ш' in the 'я' form only, as 'носи́ти' does: 'прошу́', but 'про́сиш', 'про́сить', 'про́сять'. The stress moves as well: it is on the ending in 'прошу́' and on the stem in every other form of the present.

The predicative word 'важли́во' keeps the stress of the adjective 'важли́вий': 'Це важли́ва розмо́ва.' (This is an important conversation.) and 'Це важли́во.' (This is important.) 'Необхі́дно' and 'необхі́дний' share their stress in the same way.

The other new words follow the rules of the opening units:

- In 'дозволя́ти', 'забороня́ти' and 'наполяга́ти' the 'л' and 'н' are soft before 'я'.
- In the imperative 'дозво́ль' the soft sign keeps the 'л' soft at the end of the word, and the stress stays on the stem, as in every form of 'дозво́лити'.
- In 'наді́я' [nɑˈdʲijɑ] the 'д' is soft before 'і', and 'я' after a vowel is [jɑ].
- In 'за́мість' [ˈzɑmʲisʲtʲ] the soft sign makes the 'т' soft, and the 'с' before it is said soft too.
- In 'мета́' the 'м' is hard before 'е', and the unstressed 'е' leans a little toward 'и'.
- In the present of 'пропонува́ти', '-ува-' becomes '-у-', as in 'працюва́ти': 'пропону́ю'.
- 'Гуртожи́ток', dormitory, has a fleeting 'о', so every form with an ending drops it: 'у гуртожи́тку'.
- 'Петре́', in the letter, is the vocative of the man's name 'Петро́', which replaces '-о' with '-е'. The vocative of a name in '-о' is learned with the name, since 'та́то' takes '-у' ('та́ту').
- In the loanword 'проє́кт' [prɔˈjɛkt] the 2019 spelling writes 'є' after the vowel 'о', and 'є' after a vowel is [jɛ].

culture.title: Wishes at the table
culture.text:
At a Ukrainian celebration, whether a birthday, a wedding or a family dinner, guests stand up one after another to make a toast: a short speech that ends with a wish and a drink. Many toasts are clauses with 'щоб' that stand alone, with the verb of wishing left out. They are wishes, not facts, so their verb is the past form, as in every clause with 'щоб' that has its own subject:

- 'Щоб ми всі були́ здоро́ві!' (To the health of us all!), literally 'that-would we all were healthy!'
- 'Щоб у вас усе́ було́ до́бре!' (May all go well for you!), literally 'that-would at you all was well!'
- 'Щоб ми ча́сто зустріча́лися!' (May we meet often!)

The shortest and most common toast is 'Бу́дьмо!' (Cheers!), literally 'let-us-be!'. It is the first person plural imperative of 'бу́ти', formed like 'ході́мо', and it wishes everyone at the table health and a long life. The guests often answer it with the exclamation 'Гей!'.

A wish for one person uses 'бажа́ти' with the dative and the genitive, as on a birthday: 'Бажа́ю тобі́ здоро́в’я!' The same verb closes an ordinary conversation in a shop or an office: 'Бажа́ю вам до́брого дня!' (Have a good day!) When someone sneezes, Ukrainians say 'Будь здоро́вий!' to a man and 'Будь здоро́ва!' to a woman, with the imperative 'будь' of 'бу́ти'. When a guest thanks the host for a meal, the host answers 'На здоро́в’я!' (You're welcome), literally 'for health'.

paragraphs.target: Чому́ все це? Ми хо́чемо, щоб ко́жен почува́вся тут як удо́ма. Якщо́ у вас є пита́ння, ми про́симо вас зайти́ до нас на пе́рший по́верх.
paragraphs.source: Why all this? We want everyone to feel at home here. If you have any questions, please come and see us on the first floor.
paragraphs.source_literal: Why all this? We want, that-would each felt here as at-home. If at you is questions, we ask you to-drop-in to us to first floor.

questions.prompt: Why does everyone need to know what is allowed in the dormitory?
choices: Because the rules change every week
questions.explanation: 'У на́шому гуртожи́тку живе́ бага́то люде́й, тому́ необхі́дно, щоб ко́жен знав...' The necessity is stated with 'необхі́дно' and 'щоб'.

questions.prompt: What does the dormitory ask of everyone after eleven in the evening?
choices: That nobody cooks in the kitchen
questions.explanation: 'Пі́сля одина́дцятої ве́чора ми про́симо, щоб ніхто́ не співа́в і не танцюва́в.' Friends must leave at ten, not eleven.

questions.prompt: Until what time may friends visit?
questions.explanation: 'Дру́зі мо́жуть прихо́дити до вас до деся́тої ве́чора.' 'Деся́тої' is the genitive of 'деся́та', the tenth hour.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of all these rules?
choices: That everyone should feel at home
questions.explanation: 'Ми хо́чемо, щоб ко́жен почува́вся тут як удо́ма.' The past form 'почува́вся' agrees with 'ко́жен', the subject of its own clause.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian verbs with their meanings
Match the Ukrainian words with their meanings

exercises.audio_target: Я пропону́ю, щоб ми пої́хали по́їздом.
choices: I insist that we go by train.
I suggest we go by bus.
I suggest we go by train.

exercises.prompt: What is the conjunction 'щоб' made of?
choices: 'Що', that, and the particle 'б' of the conditional
It is one root and cannot be divided
exercises.explanation: 'Щоб' is 'що' and 'б' fused into one word, as 'якби́' is 'як' and 'би'. Because it contains the particle, its clause is a conditional.

exercises.audio_target: Ма́ма хо́че, щоб ми прийшли́ ра́зом.
choices: Mom wants to come with us.
Mom wants us to come together.
Mom wants us to come tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: Oksana wants Sam to come to dinner. Which sentence does she say to him?
choices: Я хо́чу, щоб ти прийшла́ на вече́рю.
Я хо́чу, щоб ти прийшо́в на вече́рю.
exercises.explanation: Sam is to come, not Oksana, so the wish takes 'щоб' and the past form. The past form agrees with its own subject, 'ти', meaning Sam, a man: 'прийшо́в'. 'Я хо́чу прийти́' would mean that Oksana herself wants to come.

exercises.hint_source: I want you to phone me.
exercises.explanation: Another person is to act, so the clause opens with 'щоб' and has the past form 'подзвони́в'.

exercises.prompt: In 'Я хо́чу, щоб ти прийшо́в за́втра.', when is the person wanted to come?
choices: Yesterday, because 'прийшо́в' is a past form
Now, at the moment of speaking
Tomorrow: after 'щоб' the past form carries no past time
exercises.explanation: 'Щоб' contains the particle 'б', so its clause is a conditional, and in a conditional the past form shows only gender and number. 'За́втра' sets the time.

exercises.prompt_target: Тара́се, Со́фія хо́че, щоб ти ___ до не́ї.
exercises.hint_source: Taras, Sofiia wants you to drop in on her.
exercises.explanation: After 'щоб' the verb is the past form, and it agrees with its own subject, 'ти', meaning Taras: 'зайшо́в', not the feminine form that would agree with Sofiia.

exercises.prompt_target: Окса́но, та́то хо́че, щоб ти ___ ра́зом із Се́мом.
exercises.hint_source: Oksana, Dad wants you to come together with Sam.
exercises.explanation: The subject of the clause with 'щоб' is 'ти', meaning Oksana, so the past form is feminine: 'прийшла́'.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'I want to rest'?
exercises.explanation: The person who wants and the person who rests are the same, so 'хоті́ти' takes an infinitive. 'Я хо́чу, щоб ти відпочива́в.' means 'I want you to rest', and 'Я хоті́в відпочива́ти.' means 'I wanted to rest'.

exercises.prompt_target: Я вивча́ю украї́нську мо́ву, щоб ___ в Украї́ні.
exercises.hint_source: I'm learning Ukrainian to work in Ukraine.
exercises.explanation: The speaker learns and the speaker will work: the purpose has the same subject, so 'щоб' takes an infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'Я п’ю ка́ву, щоб не спа́ти.' have an infinitive after 'щоб', but 'Я говорю́ пові́льно, щоб ти все розумі́в.' the past form?
choices: The first sentence is about the present and the second about the past.
In the first the purpose has the subject of the main clause; in the second it has its own subject, 'ти', so it needs the past form.
exercises.explanation: The rule is the same as after 'хоті́ти': one subject takes the infinitive, two different subjects take 'щоб' with the past form. The past form here says nothing about time.

exercises.prompt_target: Візьми́ ку́ртку, щоб тобі́ не ___ хо́лодно.
exercises.hint_source: Take a jacket so that you don't get cold.
exercises.explanation: 'Хо́лодно' is a predicative word in a clause without a subject, so the past form is the 'воно́' form 'було́', as in 'Мені́ було́ хо́лодно'.

exercises.prompt: Which form completes 'Сього́дні я їм борщ за́мість ___.'?
exercises.explanation: 'За́мість' is a preposition that takes the genitive, and 'суп', a substance, takes '-у': 'за́мість су́пу', instead of soup.

exercises.hint_source: Instead of resting, Oksana is working.
exercises.explanation: 'За́мість того́, щоб' with an infinitive names the action that does not happen: literally 'instead of-that that-would to-rest'.

exercises.prompt_target: Сем пої́хав до Льво́ва для ___, щоб працюва́ти.
exercises.hint_source: Sam went to Lviv in order to work.
exercises.explanation: 'Для того́, щоб' is 'для' with 'того́', the genitive of 'те', which points ahead to the clause with 'щоб'.

choices: The doctor allows Sam to drink coffee.
The doctor forbids Sam to drink coffee.
The doctor forbids Sam to drink juice.

exercises.hint_source: Mom doesn't let me go for walks at night.
exercises.explanation: 'Дозволя́ти' takes the person allowed in the dative, 'мені́', and the action as an infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Which word completes 'Я прошу́ ___ прийти́.' (I'm asking you to come)?
exercises.explanation: 'Проси́ти' takes the person asked in the accusative, 'тебе́'. 'Дозволя́ти' and 'забороня́ти' take the dative instead, so the case is learned with each verb.

exercises.prompt_target: Со́фія наполяга́є на ___, щоб ми закі́нчили проє́кт.
exercises.hint_source: Sofiia insists that we finish the project.
exercises.explanation: 'Наполяга́ти' takes 'на' with the locative, and before a clause that is 'на то́му, щоб', with 'то́му', the locative of 'те'.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Він сказа́в, щоб Окса́на прийшла́.' mean?
choices: He said that Oksana had come.
He said that Oksana would come.
exercises.explanation: 'Сказа́ти' with 'щоб' passes on a request: someone wants Oksana to come. A fact would take 'що': 'Він сказа́в, що Окса́на прийшла́.' means 'He said that Oksana had come'.

exercises.prompt_target: Я сподіва́юся, ___ ти при́йдеш у неді́лю.
exercises.hint_source: I hope you'll come on Sunday.
exercises.explanation: Hope presents what is expected as a fact, so it takes 'що' and the indicative, here the perfective future 'при́йдеш'.

exercises.prompt: Which conjunction completes 'Окса́на бої́ться, ___ Сем не бу́де ві́льний.'?
exercises.explanation: A fear about what will be true takes 'що' and the indicative, here the future 'бу́де'. After 'щоб' and 'якби́' the verb would be the past form.

choices: The stem 'бо-' ends in a vowel, so the [j] of the ending is written inside the letter 'ї', which is always [ji].
exercises.explanation: 'Боя́тися' is in the second conjugation, like 'стоя́ти', 'стої́ш'. After the vowel of the stem, the ending '-иш' is written '-їш': 'бої́шся' [bɔˈjisʲːɑ].

exercises.prompt: How is the imperative 'не бі́йся' built?
choices: The stem 'бо-' takes '-й', and 'о' becomes 'і' in the closed syllable 'бій', as in 'кіт' against 'кота́'.
It is the past form of 'боя́тися' with 'не'.
It is the 'ти' form of the present without its ending.
exercises.explanation: A stem that ends in a vowel takes '-й' in the imperative, as 'чита́-' gives 'чита́й'. The '-й' closes the syllable, so 'о' becomes 'і': 'бій', then '-ся'. 'Стоя́ти' gives 'стій' in the same way.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, what does Halyna ask Oksana to tell Sam today?
choices: Not to plan anything for Sunday
exercises.explanation: Halyna says 'скажи́ йому́ сього́дні, щоб він нічо́го не планува́в на неді́лю'. Later she asks that he not buy anything, and dinner is at seven.

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, what does Sofiia forbid the team to do?
exercises.explanation: Sofiia says 'я забороня́ю вам працюва́ти вночі́'. She allows them to work at home, and Taras suggests the morning meetings.

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, what does Taras suggest after Sofiia says the director wants to know everything?
choices: That Sofiia give the team another programmer
That they finish the project on Monday
That the team meet every morning and talk about the project
exercises.explanation: Taras says 'я пропону́ю, щоб ми зустріча́лися ко́жного ра́нку й говори́ли про проє́кт'. He asked for another programmer earlier, and Sofiia had none.

exercises.prompt_source: I want you to help me. (to a man you call 'ти')
answers: Я хо́чу, щоб ти мені́ допомі́г.
Я хо́чу, щоб ти допомі́г мені́.
exercises.explanation: Two different subjects take 'щоб' with the past form, and 'допомі́г', the past form of 'допомогти́', agrees with the man addressed.

exercises.prompt_source: It's important that you sleep well. (to a woman you call 'ти')
exercises.explanation: The predicative word 'важли́во' takes 'щоб' with the past form, and 'спала́' agrees with the woman addressed.

exercises.prompt_source: I drink tea instead of coffee.
exercises.explanation: 'За́мість' takes the genitive: 'ка́ва' becomes 'ка́ви'.

exercises.prompt_source: I hope it will be warm tomorrow.
answers: Я сподіва́юся, що за́втра бу́де те́пло.
Я сподіва́юся, що бу́де те́пло за́втра.
Я сподіва́юсь, що за́втра бу́де те́пло.
Я сподіва́юсь, що бу́де те́пло за́втра.
exercises.explanation: Hope takes 'що' and the indicative, and a future event is in the future: 'бу́де те́пло'. After a vowel '-ся' may also be written '-сь'.

exercises.prompt_source: I came in order to help you. (said by a man)
We hope that you will come. (to several people)

exercises.audio_target: Я бою́ся, що він не при́йде.

exercises.hint_source: Don't be afraid, everything will be fine.
